       Line skipping in Europe     DAWN GILBERTSON/WSJ   You’ve probably seen influencer videos touting the magic VIP greeters who work at crowded European airports. It sounds like a dream in this era of messy passport lines.

   Many of you asked whether they are worth it after I weighed in on the pros and cons of airline VIP services this summer.

   So I booked SkyVIP Service for my arrival in Rome. I paid $491 for two people with a 10% discount I found online. The company’s sales pitch: Avoid long lines at the airport with our personal VIP assistance.

   My greeter, a lovely woman named Sabina, greeted my 84-year-old mom and me shortly after we deplaned. She grabbed my mom’s carry-on bag and asked if I wanted her to grab my backpack. 

   Not too long in, though, I wondered what I was paying for because there was no speeding through the airport initially. It wasn’t any fault of the service. My mom requests a wheelchair to and from gates to avoid long walks.

And it requires wheelchair passengers to take a separate van. This arrived much later than the bus. When my mom got off the van she didn’t have a wheelchair because it went to needier passengers. Sabina told us it would take 30 minutes for one to arrive.

Dawn Gilbertson
 
I Tested Another Airport VIP Service, This Time in Rome
 
Plus, cruise-ship drama, and Rome is college basketball central
 

Greetings from Rome, which is delightful anytime but especially in the off season, if you can still call it that. It’s 70 and sunny as I write this from the hotel pool to fight off jet lag before heading to the Vatican. 

 

I tried one of those VIP airport services on arrival at Rome Fiumicino after several of you asked me whether it’s worth it given the EES mess. More on that below. 

 

It’s a big college basketball weekend in Rome with Villanova and Notre Dame squaring off in the Eternal City Tip-Off to kick off the season. Villanova put up ads in baggage claim touting the school’s connection to Pope Leo, class of 1977. Wish I was going to be in the city long enough to attend.

 

In travel news this week, a residential cruise ship, The Odyssey, abruptly shut down and stranded passengers in Cambodia due to financial problems. Spain’s second high-speed train crash this year left dozens dead.

 

And JetBlue Airways executives tried to calm investors’ nerves about its long-term prospects. 

 

I’m on vacation for the next two weeks, but you’ll still see the newsletter in your inbox thanks to my colleague Jacob Passy. You will see a column from me next week so please give it a read. Let’s just say it’s the first time I brought holiday jammies on assignment.

 
 
 

Line skipping in Europe

 
 
DAWN GILBERTSON/WSJ
 

You’ve probably seen influencer videos touting the magic VIP greeters who work at crowded European airports. It sounds like a dream in this era of messy passport lines.

 

Many of you asked whether they are worth it after I weighed in on the pros and cons of airline VIP services this summer.

 

So I booked SkyVIP Service for my arrival in Rome. I paid $491 for two people with a 10% discount I found online. The company’s sales pitch: Avoid long lines at the airport with our personal VIP assistance.

 

My greeter, a lovely woman named Sabina, greeted my 84-year-old mom and me shortly after we deplaned. She grabbed my mom’s carry-on bag and asked if I wanted her to grab my backpack. 

 

Not too long in, though, I wondered what I was paying for because there was no speeding through the airport initially. It wasn’t any fault of the service. My mom requests a wheelchair to and from gates to avoid long walks.

 

Rome is one of those airports where you take a bus to passport control and baggage claim, at least on certain airlines including American. And it requires wheelchair passengers to take a separate van. This arrived much later than the bus. When my mom got off the van she didn’t have a wheelchair because it went to needier passengers. Sabina told us it would take 30 minutes for one to arrive.

 

So with my mom’s blessing, we walked to passport control. This is where being escorted started to pay off. We went through a priority line (Sabina says that’s not always allowed) that saved probably 20 minutes over the regular line. 

 

In baggage claim, she picked up a luggage cart and picked all of our bags off the belt. I can certainly do this myself. But I was grateful for the assist since I had so little sleep on the red-eye flight that my Oura ring recorded it as a nap!

 

The taxi line is where the magic happened. There must have been at least 100 people waiting to get to central Rome. There’s a fixed rate for those trips, so it’s often more attractive than a ride-share. 

 

Sabina politely maneuvered us to the front of the line in minutes with no shortage of side eye from other passengers.

 

I certainly wouldn’t plunk down $500 for two on most trips. But, as with the airline VIP services, there are special occasions and travel partners and business trips where you have to hit the ground running. For those it can make sense. 

 

Do some math to help you decide if money is not unlimited. Which travel upgrade would bring you more joy? American dangled a last-minute upgrade to premium economy on my nine-hour flight to Rome for $296 per person. I was ready to jump on it until I found out it was a middle seat.

 

My mom, meanwhile, can’t stop raving about the VIP airport experience.

 

This is an edition of the WSJ Travel newsletter, a weekly source of inspiration and advice for navigating your vacations and business trips, along with the latest travel news. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

Notes From the Road ✈️

 
 
PETER ARKLE FOR WSJ
 

• Don’t get too excited about all those new airline frills. It’ll probably be a while before they’re on your next flight.

 

• Been there, done that at St. Andrews? Check out Scotland’s remote, primitive courses.

 

• Our guide to finding a great meal after midnight in New York.

 

• New England doesn’t own the market on fall foliage. Virginia’s Shenandoah National Park and Shenandoah Valley are equally majestic.

Travel Math 🧮

 
$67.82
 

Frontier Airlines’ fare revenue per passenger in the third quarter, compared with $39.74 a year earlier, a whopping 71% increase.

 
 
 

And We Quote 💬

 

“A few are shellshocked because they spent the majority of their nest eggs to be here, and don’t know how or where they’ll live.”

 

— Randy Cassingham, a passenger on the residential cruise ship The Odyssey, which abruptly stopped sailing this week.

 
 
 

Travel-arious 🤣

 

I snorted when I saw this Threads post about luxury travel ads on Hulu and thought a lot of you could relate, too.

 

“I just had an ad for the Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection on Hulu and I just want them to know that if I could afford that I wouldn’t have (expletive) Hulu with ads.”

 
 
 

Cheers and Jeers 🤷

 

Cheers to AeroLOPA, the website and app that offers detailed airline seat maps including grades for each seat. It steered me away from an extra legroom seat I had booked on an American 777-200. The website is free but there’s a fee for the app.

 

Jeers to the shortage of airport wheelchair attendants. We had to wait 20 minutes for one at Miami International Airport ahead of the flight to Rome despite having reservations.
